questions.q: Can a single 3-wire intracortical electrode enable near-conversational synthetic speech for individuals with locked-in syndrome, and what are the key factors limiting current performance?
questions.answer: The participant achieved improved vowel production (hit rate 45%→70%, endpoint error 435→233 Hz) across 25 sessions with a single 3-wire electrode, but performance remains limited to a 3-vowel repertoire. Key limiting factors include the small vowel set, dependence on practice, lack of consonant exploration, and the single-participant case design. The authors concede that improved decoding techniques and more recording sites could yield larger performance gains.

questions.q: Q1. What is the total delay from neural signal to audio output (the "within 50 ms" claim)? Give the abstract sentence.
questions.answer: The abstract says the synthesizer gave immediate auditory feedback within 50 ms. The Methods section gives the measured delay as 30–70 ms, with an estimated average of 50 ms.

questions.q: Q2. How is a "hit" defined in the three-vowel task: target region size, dwell time (500 ms?), maximum trial duration (6 s?)?
questions.answer: A hit required decoded formants to enter and remain in the circular target region for 500 ms; the region spanned approximately 150 Hz in F1 and 300 Hz in F2. Trials ended on a hit or after 6 seconds, whichever came first.

questions.q: Q3. Is there any attractor force, assistance or bias toward targets in the real-time decoder? Describe and quote.
questions.answer: Yes. A small attractor force operated inside a target region to help keep output there after entry; it did not affect the formant trajectory outside target regions.

questions.q: Q4. Is chance level of hit rate given anywhere? Is a no-neural or shuffled control given?
questions.answer: not stated for the hit-rate chance level or for a no-neural/shuffled control of the real-time vowel task. The paper does report random-firing Monte Carlo simulations for tuning-statistics analyses, not as a task-performance control.

questions.q: Q5. Exactly how are hit rate 45% to 70% and endpoint error 435 Hz to 233 Hz computed: first vs last block within a session averaged across sessions? How many sessions/blocks/trials enter? What statistical test?
questions.answer: These are first-block versus last-block averages across sessions, not session 1 versus session 25: Figure 7 averages block performance across all 25 sessions. There were 1–4 blocks and 5–34 attempted productions per session, but total blocks/trials are not stated; the block trends were tested with a t-test of the null hypothesis of zero slope versus block number (p<0.05).

questions.q: Q6. Where is the electrode implanted (brain area), when, and what is the participant's condition and age?
questions.answer: It was implanted in a speech-related area of the left precentral gyrus, near the boundary between premotor and primary motor cortex. The male participant was 26 and had locked-in syndrome after a brain-stem stroke at 16; implantation was at age 21, about five years after the stroke and 38 months before the study began.

questions.q: Q7. Describe the wireless system: FM transmission, receivers, number of channels, power (inductive?), sampling rate.
questions.answer: The two-channel Neurotrophic Electrode signals were amplified under the scalp and sent across it by FM radio; two additional coils received the FM signals, and the received signals were amplified again. The subcutaneous electronics were inductively powered by a temporary head-mounted power coil, and the channels were sampled at 30303 Hz (as printed in text.txt).

questions.q: Q8. What exactly does the paper claim as "first" (quote the sentence with "first")?
questions.answer: The authors claim this was, to their knowledge, the first successful use of a permanently installed telemetric implant for real-time control of an external device.

questions.q: Q9. How many units/clusters were used in the real-time decoder per session? Were units selected per session?
questions.answer: The number used by the real-time decoder per session is not stated. Yes, units were selected separately for each session using a significant functional relationship to the intended sequence (multiple linear regression F-test, p<0.05); the 56 clusters reported elsewhere are for the offline analysis, not the per-session decoder count.

questions.q: Q10. Did the decoder change across sessions (re-trained each session)? Did performance across sessions (session 1 vs 25) improve, or only within session blocks?
questions.answer: The Kalman filter parameters were trained at the start of every session. Performance improved both within sessions and across days: average endpoint error declined significantly over the 25 sessions, although an exact session-1-versus-session-25 value comparison is not stated; the reported 45% to 70% hit-rate change is first-to-last block across sessions.

questions.q: Q11. Did the offline analysis (ridge regression r=.69/.68) use cross-validation? Which data?
questions.answer: The plotted r=.69/.68 reconstruction was an offline ridge fit (ridge parameter .01) from one recording, using the whole dataset for illustration, so those plotted correlations are not identified as cross-validated. Separately, the paper reports two-fold cross-validation within each of eight 63.4-second attempted-speech sessions, averaging across sessions, for its ensemble analyses (56 spike clusters; F1 r=.49 and F2 r=.57).

questions.q: Q12. Is any listener or intelligibility evaluation of the synthesized vowels reported?
questions.answer: not stated

questions.q: Q13. Do the authors state any limitation about the two-dimensional formant space, consonants, or number of electrodes? Quote.
questions.answer: The task used a two-dimensional F1–F2 space, but the paper does not explicitly call that dimensionality a limitation. It does state that the demonstrated ability was limited to a small set of vowels, proposes consonant production with improved methods, and notes use of a single 3-wire electrode.

questions.q: Q14. What were the training targets during the one-minute vowel mimicry protocol (the participant listened to and attempted to mimic a stimulus sequence?) and was any audio from the participant used?
questions.answer: The participant attempted to speak in synchrony with a predictable auditory sequence of 1-second UH, IY, A, or OO vowels, with 300 ms formant transitions; the stimulus formant trajectories were aligned with neural data for training. No audio or visual feedback was given, and whether participant-produced audio was recorded or otherwise used is not stated.

questions.q: Q1
questions.answer: Yes. The external Brown Wireless Device attaches to the existing percutaneous pedestal, leaving the through-skin pedestal in place; wireless transmission replaces the recording cable between the pedestal and acquisition equipment.

questions.q: Q2
questions.answer: Two 96-channel arrays (192 electrodes total) were wirelessly sampled at 20 kS/s per electrode during one continuous 24-hour home recording (one day).

questions.q: Q3
questions.answer: In the Grid Task, T5 had 96.1% cabled versus 97.9% wireless success and 1.62 versus 1.81 bps, while T10 had 91.6% versus 94.8% success and 1.51 bps in both conditions.

questions.q: Q4
questions.answer: Two participants (T5 and T10).

questions.q: Q5
questions.answer: Yes. The system relied on percutaneous wired connections, with subcutaneous wires joining the arrays to percutaneous titanium pedestals; the authors say future work will evaluate wireless or fully implantable systems.

questions.q: Q6
questions.answer: T15 used it independently at home for 19 months (>3,800 h); prompted word-copy decoding reached 99.2% word accuracy (125,000-word vocabulary), while personal use averaged 56 words/min and 92% of sentences were rated at least mostly correct.
